PLD methods, particularly those based on logical expressions, are increasingly being applied to datasets that are represented as tables. A key challenge in PLD is the efficient identification of complex patterns within large datasets. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach called Prefix-Tree Based Probabilistic Logic Learning (PTB-PLL). This method utilizes prefix trees to store logical expressions, and utilizes information from the parent nodes to minimize the computational overhead. Additionally, we implement techniques to minimize the storage space required for the prefix tree. Our experimental results using real-world datasets demonstrate that PTB-PLL outperforms existing PLD methods in efficiency. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the time complexity of PTB-PLL, and our findings suggest that it has polynomial complexity. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric called Average Distance (AD) to evaluate the quality of the learned logic and demonstrate its suitability for PLD tasks. Our experiments show that PTB-PLL consistently produces high-quality results, and its performance is comparable to that of the best existing PLD methods. Notably, PTB-PLL is the first PLD method to provide guaranteed performance guarantees for learning disjunctive logic programs. We also investigate the use of PTB-PLL for detecting frequent itemsets, and our results indicate that it has potential in this area as well. Overall, our experimental results suggest that PTB-PLL is a highly efficient and effective PLD method for learning disjunctive logic programs from datasets. of various NLP applications, encompassing both simple and complex tasks, thanks to powerful tools that enable efficient processing.  Despite the significance of these tools, their development is hindered by a major obstacle: ensuring safety during training.  Current approaches typically employ either a narrow, task-specific safety method or a broad, task-agnostic safety method, neither of which offers complete safety guarantees.  We introduce a novel safety method for neural networks that combines both specific and general safety measures.  This new method, known as the Safety Gradient Descent approach, utilizes two distinct neural networks: one for inferring safe patterns and the other for performing the actual task.  The Safety Gradient Descent approach adapts the first neural network to identify safe patterns within the input data.  It then adjusts the second neural network's parameters to follow these patterns, effectively minimizing the risk of safe failures.  We tested the Safety Gradient Descent approach on multiple tasks and found it to outperform existing safety methods, such as Soft Actor Critic, on a set of challenging control tasks.  We also applied this approach to a complex natural language processing task and achieved significant results in reducing failure rates in a challenging text-based game.  Our findings demonstrate the potential of the Safety Gradient Descent approach for enhancing the reliability of safety methods and paving the way for more effective safety measures in the future. In this study, we investigate the stability and learning efficiency of transformer-based models and introduce a new paradigm called the Transformer with Transformer Encoder (TTE). When applied to real-world settings, our technique outperforms other methods in terms of both computational efficiency and image quality.
